blocks.text: The other passage on the kore, Ierem. XVII, 11. קרא דגר ולא ילך, is rendered thus in Greek: Ἐφώνησεν πέρδιξ, συνήγαγεν ἃ οὐκ ἔτεκεν [Ephōnēsen perdix, synēgagen ha ouk eteken], "The partridge cried out, it gathered what it did not bring forth." The words ἐφώνησεν πέρδιξ [ephōnēsen perdix] are a double rendering of the word קרא, which some read as kara and others as kore; the former rendered it ἐφώνησεν [ephōnēsen], the latter πέρδιξ [perdix] ^{(3)}. The latter rendering is followed by Jerome, the Syriac, the Arabic, the Hebrews and all the more recent writers, as though these words referred to the common partridge. And this is explained in various ways. For there are those who assert that the partridge steals the eggs of others, incubates them, and claims the chicks hatched from them as its own. Epiphanius, in the Physiologus, chapter 9: Οὐκ ἀρκεῖ αὐτῇ τῆς ἰδίας γαστρὸς ὁ τόκος, ἀλλὰ κλέπτουσα τὰ ὠὰ τῶν ἀλλοτρίων φέρει αὐτὰ ἐπὶ τὴν νεοττίαν αὐτῆς [Ouk arkei autē tēs idias gastros ho tokos, alla kleptousa ta ōa tōn allotriōn pherei auta epi tēn neottian autēs]; "The offspring of her own womb does not suffice her, but she snatches the eggs of others and carries them to her own nest." Eustathius, on the Hexaemeron, p. 29: Ἀλλότρια δὲ κλέπτων ὠὰ νεοσσοποιεῖ [Allotria de kleptōn ōa neossopoiei]; "It steals the eggs of others and hatches [II, 638] them." Ambrose, in the Hexaemeron, book 6, chapter 3: "We know the partridge to be crafty, for it snatches the eggs of another, that is, of another partridge, and warms them with its own body." And in the Letter to Sabinus, where he expounds the passage of Jeremiah at length: "Some have thought that this too should be applied to the nature of the partridge, because it snatches the eggs of others and warms them with its own body, and by this fraud seeks to acquire the offspring of others." Philastrius, On Heresies, in the Preface: "We must recognize that the enemy of the human race was not undeservedly compared by the prophet Jeremiah to the partridge, which, since it suffers barrenness, often secretly sits on the young of others and then warms and claims them as its own children." Cassiodorus, Variae, book 2, Letter 14: "Partridges too have the custom of making good their lost eggs at the loss of another mother, so as to repair the hardship of their own bereavement by adopting another's brood." Isidore, Orig. book 12, ch. 7: "The partridge is so deceitful that it snatches another's eggs and warms them." Damir, in the chapter الحجل [al-ḥajal], or On the partridge: والانثي اذا اصيب بيضها قصدت عش غيرها وغلتها علي بيضها وتسرقه وتحضنه [wa-l-unthā idhā uṣība bayḍuhā qaṣadat ʿushsha ghayrihā wa-ghallathā ʿalā bayḍihā wa-tasriquhu wa-taḥḍunuhu] "And the female, when her egg has been spoiled, invades the nest of another partridge, and substitutes for her own egg one stolen by fraud, and warms it." So he writes; I confess I do not sufficiently understand it. For I do not see how a partridge could steal the eggs of others, since it cannot do this with its beak, nor does it have toes suited to the purpose. Therefore the great author on Solinus, on page 150, not undeservedly brings a charge against Pliny for having reported that partridges carry their eggs elsewhere, since their nature does not allow this, and the contrary can be established from Aristotle.

Accordingly, the Hebrews will seem to have written more cautiously. For they do not say that the partridge carries off the eggs of others, but that it sits in another's nest. R. Selomo on 1 Sam. XXVI, 20: הקורא עוף ששמו קורא ובלעז פרד״יז וכן קורא דגר ולא ילד ומרדף אחר קיני שאר עופות ויושב על ביציהם "Kore is a bird which is so called in Hebrew, and in the vernacular perdix [partridge], of which it is said in Jeremiah: „The kore gathered, and did not bring forth“; because it pursues the nests of other birds in order to sit on their eggs." And Porta coeli, fol. 29. d.: הוא רובץ על ביצי העוף אחר ומחמם אותם "It sits on the eggs of another bird and warms them." So too Kimchi on Jeremiah. But the same author, in his [col. 85] Lexicon, asserts that the partridge first gathers the eggs of others and afterwards sits on them as if they were its own: הוא מאסף ביצי עוף אחר ורובץ עליהם כאלו הם שלו. However that may be, this too is hardly very likely, that a partridge, however much it wished, should sit in another's nest, since the true mother of the eggs would by no means allow it. These things, then, are highly paradoxical.
